correctness.rationale: The equation implies (a^p)^2=a^p and a^pa=a. Since a commutes with e=a^p, (a−e)^p=0, and a−e lies in eAe. Conversely e+x gives a solution and has p-th power e; hence the parametrization is bijective. The diagonal of x vanishes. The element e d_S+(1−e)(1−d_S) intertwines d_S and e and has unit diagonal. The orbit–stabilizer count in 1+J(P) therefore gives q^{c_P(S)} choices for e, because exactly the crossing entries are forbidden in the stabilizer. Its corner is the incidence algebra on S, with the induced order, and the empty corner contributes one. Partitioning strict pairs into inside S, outside S, and crossing gives the low-height result when every chain has at most p vertices. On the chain of p+1 vertices only the full corner has a restriction: the product of the p successive entries must vanish. Hence the number subtracted is exactly (q−1)^p q^{binom(p,2)}. Independently, for any taller induced corner one can make the endpoint entry of x^p equal 1 by using only the chosen p successive edges of a chain; it is thus a nonzero degree-p polynomial, giving the uniform bound p q^{m(S)−1}. Terms can attain q^{m(P)} only for unrestricted corners whose complements contain no comparable pair, which gives H_p(P). At height p+1, the chain-ending rank strictly increases and takes all p+1 values on every maximum chain, so a rank level is an antichain meeting each such chain. At greater height an antichain cannot remove more than one vertex from a maximum chain. These bounds also apply to edgeless P (where the error is zero). The chain assertion in frozen verify.py line 53 is not reached: its comparison list uses range(n) rather than range(n−1). A separate bounded direct replay tested the closed formula at (p,n)=(2,2),(2,3),(3,3),(3,4), obtaining counts 7,43,136,4996 and threshold subtractions 2 and 216; the symbolic product test proves the general result regardless of the dead assertion.
